analysis.one_liner: Bans the pesticide chlorpyrifos from all food and farm uses nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban chlorpyrifos, a pesticide linked to brain harm in children, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to cancel the registration of chlorpyrifos, an insecticide used on food crops, immediately ban the sale and use of any remaining stock, and strip the legal limits that allow chlorpyrifos residue on food. The EPA had been moving toward such a ban, but the bill was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers and rural residents who live near sprayed fields, and families—especially young children—exposed through food residues and drinking water. Chlorpyrifos is an organophosphate insecticide linked to neurological and developmental harm in children, and the bill would have removed it from food and farms outright.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to cancel the registration of all uses of chlorpyrifos immediately upon enactment, declaring the pesticide to cause unreasonable adverse effects on the environment, including dietary risks to humans.
Prohibits the continued sale and use of existing stocks of chlorpyrifos, so products already on shelves could not be sold or sprayed.
Requires the EPA to revoke the 'tolerances' that legally allow chlorpyrifos residue on food, removing it from the food supply, and bars the EPA from ever reregistering it.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers that make chlorpyrifos lose a major product line, and growers of crops like fruits, vegetables, almonds, and corn lose a cheap, widely used insecticide and would need substitutes that may cost more or be less effective.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and farmers who spray it

drawbacks.text: Farmers would lose a broadly effective, inexpensive insecticide with no equally cheap substitute for some pests, potentially raising production costs and prices for fruits, vegetables, and nuts.

The bill orders the ban by legislative flat rather than the normal EPA risk-assessment process, bypassing the case-by-case scientific review and comment process that usually governs pesticide cancellations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes—protecting children's brain development and farmworkers who face the heaviest exposure—were large, and substitutes for chlorpyrifos exist for most uses. The main real costs fall on growers and the manufacturer, not on consumers' access to food, so the public benefit outweighed the cost; the bill's weakness was procedural, in legislating a chemical ban instead of letting EPA's science review run its course.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce committees and their subcommittees, and no one ever scheduled a hearing or a vote, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 25, 2017 by Rep. Nydia Velazquez with 61 cosponsors, 60 Democrats and 1 Republican.

It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and within two weeks was further referred to subcommittees on Environment and on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research.
No further action was ever taken—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chlorpyrifos manufacturers and the growers who continued spraying it were better off, because the pesticide stayed legal for another two years while the bill sat untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide makers and growers who spray it

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cancel chlorpyrifos's registration, ban existing stock, and revoke food residue tolerances.

for.name: 61 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the chlorpyrifos ban.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Scott Pruitt (EPA Administrator)
against.what_they_did: Two months before the bill was introduced, reversed the Obama-era EPA proposal to ban chlorpyrifos on food, keeping the pesticide legal and removing the regulatory pressure the bill sought to lock in.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic—60 of 61 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican—and the Republican-led committees that controlled the bill never acted on it.

industries.industry: Pesticide manufacturers (notably Dow, the maker of chlorpyrifos)
industries.note: The bill would have immediately canceled the registration of one of the most widely used insecticides, wiping out its domestic sales. The industry's interest in keeping chlorpyrifos on the market ran directly against the health interests of farmworkers and children, and the pesticide stayed legal because the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Fruit, vegetable, and nut growers who use chlorpyrifos
industries.note: Growers would have lost a cheap, effective insecticide against major crop pests and faced the cost of switching to alternatives. Their exposure to the chemical, and their workers' exposure, also created health costs the ban would have ended.
